title: Key squares
summary: King and pawn against king: the square that decides the ending.
part.keySquares.title: Key squares
part.keySquares.summary: The squares that, once the king stands on one, make sure the pawn queens.
part.opposition.title: The opposition opens the way
part.opposition.summary: How the king reaches a key square with the black king in the way, and the mistake of the hasty pawn.
part.defend.title: The defender's side
part.defend.summary: King in front of the pawn and the opposition: that is how Kramnik held the draw.
step.t_count: The black king is far away, in the corner. Think: where must the white king go so that the e4 pawn is sure to queen, whatever the black king does?
step.t_count.hint1: Don't look at the pawn, look at the squares in front of it. Two ranks ahead, some squares decide everything.
step.intro: Every pawn has key squares. This e4-pawn has three: d6, e6 and f6, two ranks ahead of it. If my king steps on one of them, the pawn queens, whatever the black king does and whoever is to move. Averbakh taught that the king leads the pawn the way a father leads his child across the street: he goes in front.
step.count: The count is simple. Pawn up to the fourth rank: three key squares, two ranks ahead. Pawn on the fifth or sixth: six squares, the two ranks ahead, as here with the pawn on e5. On the seventh, the neighbouring squares on the seventh and eighth. The rook pawn is another story, and has a lesson of its own.
step.why: See why the key square decides. My king is on e6, in front of the pawn. If Black is to move, the black king has to step aside: Kd8 and I go to f7; Kf8 and I go to d7. And if I am to move? Then I push the pawn: e5. The black king still has no way out. On the key square, the win does not depend on who moves.
step.keyWin: Your turn. White to play. The king is already on the key square; take the pawn to the seventh rank.
step.keyWin.hint: With the king on e6, the pawn can advance. Then, when the black king gives up one side, take the seventh-rank square on the other side: f7 or d7.
step.keyWin.done: That's it. The pawn reached the seventh without check, with the king beside it. There is no defence left.
step.t_averbakh: The white king is already close, but the black king blocks the way. How does the white king make its way to the sixth rank without touching the pawn?
step.t_averbakh.hint1: Put the kings face to face with one square between them, and see what is left for the black king.
step.front: The king is not always on the key square yet. Here the pawn is still on c2, and the key squares are b4, c4 and d4. My king on d4 already holds one of them, but the black king blocks the way. The tool for moving forward is the opposition: kings face to face, one square between them, and the other side to move.
step.tool: White to play and win. Use the opposition to push the black king back, step to the next key square and repeat, until your king reaches the sixth rank.
step.tool.hint: Put your king face to face with the black king, one square between them. When he gives up one side, go forward on the other.
step.tool.done: Very good. King on the sixth rank, in front of the pawn: now it queens, and you did not even need to touch the pawn.
step.early: The most common mistake in this ending is the hasty pawn. Here, if I play d4, I throw the win away: the black king stops on d5, in front of it, takes the opposition and holds the draw. The pawn stays. The king goes in front, to a key square.
step.earlyMove: White to play and win. Which is the move: king or pawn?
step.earlyMove.hint: Not the pawn yet. Put the king on one of c4, d4 or e4.
step.earlyMove.done: Exactly. King on the key square, pawn behind it, safe. From here it is the technique you already know.
step.t_kramnik: Now you defend. The white king and pawn look strong. Where must the black king stand so that the pawn never queens?
step.t_kramnik.hint1: Stay on the pawn's file and think of the opposition the other way round: you are the one facing the white king.
step.defend: Now the other side. Kamsky against Kramnik, Nice 2009: after the rooks came off, Kramnik, with Black, reached this position. The black king stays in front of the pawn and takes the opposition when the white king comes forward. If the pawn checks on the seventh, the king steps in front of it: stalemate.
step.defendMove: Black to play and draw. Keep the white king out of the key squares.
step.defendMove.hint: Stay on the pawn's file. When the white king reaches the sixth, face him; when the pawn checks, step in front of it.
step.defendMove.done: Perfect. Now only Ke6 keeps the pawn, and that is stalemate, as in the game. That is how Kramnik held the draw.
step.recap: Three rules to take with you. First: count the pawn's key squares; winning means getting into one of them. Second: the king goes first and the pawn waits. Third: the opposition is the tool for reaching the key square, not the goal. For the defender, the mirror image: king in front of the pawn and the opposition, always.
step.finish: Now play until you queen. King in front, key square, and only then the pawn.
ex.e01: White to play and win. The e4-pawn has three key squares. Occupy one of them.
ex.e01.hint: The key squares are two ranks ahead of the pawn: d6, e6 and f6.
ex.e01.solution: Kd6 or Ke6: the two key squares the king can reach. With the king there, the pawn queens no matter what.
ex.e02: White to play and win. Where is the key square the king can reach?
ex.e02.hint: The pawn is on g3; count two ranks up.
ex.e02.solution: Kg5 or Kf5. The key squares of the g3-pawn are f5, g5 and h5, and the king reaches two of them in one move.
ex.e03: White to play and win. King move or pawn move?
ex.e03.hint: With the pawn on the fifth, there are six key squares: c6, d6, e6 and the three on the seventh.
ex.e03.solution: Kc6 or Kd6, to a key square. The push d6? lets the black king stop on d7 with the opposition, and it ends in stalemate: only a draw.
ex.e04: White to play and win. Here only one move is right.
ex.e04.hint: The king is already on the sixth rank, beside the pawn. See what the pawn does without giving check.
ex.e04.solution: e7! The pawn reaches the seventh without check, and the black king has to leave: after ...Kf7 comes Kd7 and the pawn queens. Any king move lets the black king reach e7, in front of the pawn.
ex.e05: White to play and win. Only one move keeps the win.
ex.e05.hint: The key squares of the e4-pawn are d6, e6 and f6. The pawn is no help right now.
ex.e05.solution: Ke5! The king takes the opposition and, next move, enters a key square. The push e5? lets the black king stop on d7, facing yours, with the opposition: a draw.
ex.e06: White to play and win. The opposition or the key square?
ex.e06.hint: Averbakh said it: the opposition is the means, the key square is the end. If you can get in without it, get in.
ex.e06.solution: Kc5! Straight to the door of the key squares b6, c6 and d6; next move the king occupies one of them. Taking the opposition with Ke4 only draws.
ex.e07: White to play and win. The black king blocks the direct road.
ex.e07.hint: The key squares of the d4-pawn are c6, d6 and e6. The black king does not cover all three.
ex.e07.solution: Ke6!, the key square the black king left open when it went to c7. Kc5 and Ke5 also win, going round; only retreating the king draws.
ex.e08: White to play and win. Careful: the black king is in the corner.
ex.e08.hint: With a knight pawn and the king in the corner, advancing with check can stalemate. King first.
ex.e08.solution: Kf7!, to the key square, and only then g6 and g7, with the king beside the pawn. Kh6 and Kf6 also win, but Kf5? or Kh5? leave the key square and only draw.
ex.e09: Gligorić against Fischer, 1959. Black to play and draw. Only one move holds.
ex.e09.hint: Do not go to the seventh rank: there the white king takes the opposition. Stay on the eighth, in front of the pawn.
ex.e09.solution: Kb8! Only then, when the white king comes up, Black takes the opposition: Kc5 Kc7 or Kb5 Kb7. That is what Fischer played, and the white king never reached the key squares a6, b6 and c6.
ex.e10: A position by Jan Drtina, 1908. White to play and win. The direct road does not work.
ex.e10.hint: The key squares are b5, c5 and d5. Through the centre the black king gets there first; try the other side of the pawn.
ex.e10.solution: Kc2!, then Kb3, Kb4 and, with the opposition on c4, the king enters b5. Down the d-file the black king reaches c6, takes the opposition and draws.
ex.e11: White to play and win. Only one king move keeps the win.
ex.e11.hint: The black king covers c4 and d4. Go up the side, where it cannot reach, and use the opposition.
ex.e11.solution: Kb3! and, after ...Kc5, Kc3 with the opposition. When the black king gives way, the white king enters b4, a key square. Pushing the pawn or going up through c3 at once lets the black king take the opposition.
ex.e12: Golombek against Pomar, 1946. White to play and win. The most stubborn defence is the corner.
ex.e12.hint: The black king wants h8, to be stalemated when the pawn checks. Take the king to h6 and advance the pawn only with the king beside it.
ex.e12.solution: Kh6!, ...Kh8, g6, ...Kg8, g7 and, after ...Kf7, Kh7: the pawn queens. Kf6 also wins, but after ...Kh7 it has to come back with Kf7 and Kg6.
key.count: Counting the key squares: for the e4-pawn, d6, e6 and f6, two ranks ahead. On the fifth and sixth, six squares; on the seventh, the neighbours on the seventh and eighth.
key.averbakh: Averbakh's example: the white king is already on the key square d4; the opposition is the tool for advancing to the sixth rank.
key.opposition: The opposition is a means, not an end: Kc5 wins by going to the key square; taking the opposition with Ke4 draws. Averbakh's remark, via Wikipedia.
key.drtina: Jan Drtina, 1908: any key square, by any route. Kc2! goes round the side of the pawn the black king cannot reach.
key.gligoricFischer: Gligorić–Fischer, Candidates 1959: Black draws with Kb8!, keeping the white king out of a6, b6 and c6.
key.kamskyKramnik: Kamsky–Kramnik, Nice 2009: after 125.Kxc6, Kramnik drew with the king in front of the pawn and the opposition, down to stalemate.
history: The idea of the key square, or critical square, is the way of teaching this ending that Yuri Averbakh left us: instead of calculating, you count the squares and know where the king has to go. The image of the father crossing the street ahead of his child is his. In 1908, Jan Drtina showed that a key square can be reached by any route, even going round behind the pawn. In 1959, at the Candidates Tournament, Fischer held the draw against Gligorić with a single king move, Kb8. In 1968, Najdorf lost to Panno because the white king reached the key square g7 of a rook pawn. In 2009, Kramnik drew against Kamsky, blindfold, with his king in front of the pawn down to stalemate. Karsten Müller and Frank Lamprecht summed up the win in three conditions: king in front of the pawn, the opposition and king on the sixth rank; two of them are enough.
practice: Now the real ending: king on d2, pawn on g2, and the black king waiting. Count the key squares, lead with the king and queen the pawn. Pick your pace and go.
